titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State

div.head: 398. Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State
div.p: 2862. Subject: Ambassador Middendorf’s visit to Paraguay.

2. Begin summary. During his July 22–24 visit Ambassador Middendorf was given an extraordinarily warm welcome as the first high-ranking representative of the Reagan administration to visit Paraguay. President Stroessner returned early from a trip to the Chaco expressly to receive him. In that meeting as in those with the Foreign Minister and several other senior GOP officials the Ambassador emphasized the high priority which the administration places on improved relations with Latin America including the Southern Cone and specifically Paraguay, our development plans and hope for support in the troubled Caribbean Basin, the need for cooperation against international terrorism, OAS budget concerns, and the importance of the private sector’s role in national and regional development. On all these subjects he was assured of Paraguayan support. Ambassador Middendorf also visited a major OAS/IDB rural development project, and met with a group of private businessmen. Press coverage of the visit was extensive and uniformly favorable. End summary.

3. Meeting with the President. President Stroessner returned early from a visit to the Chaco region especially to receive Ambassador Middendorf, accompanied by Ambassador Lane, for nearly an hour early on July 24. Ambassador Middendorf conveyed the warm greetings of President Reagan and Secretary Haig to the President and people of Paraguay, and their intention to give the highest priority to good relations with the countries of Latin America. The President expressed his great appreciation of these greetings, reciprocated them, and said that close relations with the U.S. are of historical importance to Paraguay. He recalled that Paraguay had joined with the U.S. in sending troops to the Dominican Republic in 1965 in its desire to help avoid another Cuba in Latin America. Paraguay is a homogeneous, firmly anti-communist country which seeks liberty with order. This approach has brought good results to the country
which is developing rapidly. Ambassador Middendorf responded that the U.S. values its close, historical ties with Paraguay, appreciates its support in the Dominican crisis, and recognizes the rapid growth and stability of this country with a minimum of social disparities. He praised the export-oreinted, private sector orientation of Paraguay which has been emulated by other countries. In this connection he stressed the contribution that American companies like Allis-Chalmers (a major bidder on the Yacyreta hydroelectric project) can make in the development of Paraguay and as “goodwill ambassadors.” As illustrative of the new U.S. approach to the developing world he provided copies of his address on “The Reagan Administration and Economic Development in the Third World” and USTR’s “statement on U.S. trade policy” which the President said he would read carefully.

4. Ambassador Middendorf reviewed briefly for the President our hopes for cooperative action to help in the Caribbean Basin, not as an anti-Castro effort but rather to strengthen the economies of that region. He said we hope for the support of Paraguay and other countries of the hemisphere in this effort. Stroessner replied “of course”, and went on to elaborate his strong views on the danger of communism and the need to deal with it firmly. Ambassador Middendorf said that we will keep GOP informed on Caribbean Basin planning and that we will wish to consult with Paraguay and other countries as it progresses.

5. Noting a reference by President Stroessner to communist support of terrorism, Ambassador Middendorf said that the U.S. believes strongly that terrorist attacks against independent countries must be stopped and that nations must cooperate to this end. The U.S. will do our share. Stroessner responded that this is necessary since communism and Moscow are against us. He added that the communists kill people and then invoke human rights to defend themselves as in Nicaragua and Cuba. He added that he supports human rights and that his government doesn’t kill anyone. Indeed it protects its citizens.
As a result Paraguayans are better off. The only ones who criticize him are communists. He then mentioned once observing communist propaganda in the lobby of a hotel in San Francisco. Ambassador Middendorf commented that in a democracy like the United States such manifestations are of course permitted but the communists are a fringe group of no real importance.

6. Observing that the administration wants improved relations with the countries of the Southern Cone, Ambassador Middendorf referred to the change of policy on votes in the MDBs. President Stroessner replied that his government is very pleased with the policies of the President and Secretary Haig. He went on to criticize the role of a former Ambassador (clearly Ambassador White) in Paraguay, particularly for his intimate association with the unrecognized opposition parties; while avoiding direct criticism of the former President, Stroessner then observed that some officials around Carter benefited communism. Avoiding any direct response to those remarks, Ambassador Middendorf said only that President Reagan and his administration have the fullest confidence in Ambassador Lane.

7. Ambassador Middendorf expressed U.S. appreciation for Paraguay’s support on efforts to reduce the OAS budget and to effect a better sharing of the organization’s costs, two thirds of which the U.S. now bears. Stroessner replied that our concerns on the budget are warranted, but that the U.S. must not relinquish its firm position of leadership on which small countries threatened by communism, like El Salvador, depend. He concluded the discussion by expressing his strong personal opinion that the Governments of South Africa and Taiwan deserve our support because they are firmly anti-communist. He said we must not support SWAPO and allow another Rhodesia. Ambassador Middendorf made no comment.

8. Meeting with Foreign Minister. In a meeting with Foreign Minister Alberto Nogues on July 23, Ambassador Middendorf stressed the high priority which the President and Secretary of State place on improved relations with Latin America. Nogues expressed his appreciation of this policy and said he very much hopes to
call on Secretary Haig in Washington prior to the UNGA. Middendorf promised to look into the possibilities for such a meeting but pointed out the scheduling problems. He then proceeded to deal at length with the issues of the Caribbean Basin Plan, international terrorism, OAS budget matters, and the importance of the role of the private sector in development. Nogues took note of the developmental as distinct from anti-Cuban thrust of the new initiative in the Caribbean, but stressed Paraguay’s particular concern with Cuba’s disturbing role throughout Latin America. He welcomed Middendorf’s promise of future consultations with the GOP as Caribbean Basin planning progresses, and expressed confidence that Paraguay will be receptive and supportive. On terrorism, Nogues agreed that international cooperation is indispensable—as is U.S. leadership. He said that the Stroessner government has sought to provide peace and stability to permit development. Despite past political differences, Paraguay has always been a loyal friend of the U.S. Paraguay shares and attempts to emulate U.S. democratic ideals, but it must be recognized that some countries are able to reach those goals faster than others due to special historical and political realities. When Ambassador Middendorf mentioned the recent change of U.S. voting policy in the MDBs as a recognition of human rights progress in Paraguay, Nogues coupled appreciation of that decision with the statement that Paraguay should really never had been included in the same category with the other Southern Cone countries in the first place since it has fortunately avoided their political problems and is perfecting its democratic institutions.

9. Referring to OAS projects in Paraguay, Ambassador Middendorf said the U.S. welcomes GOP efforts and support to reduce the OAS headquarters bureaucracy in order to continue sound programs in the field, and to reduce the U.S. share of the normal budget by 1 percent per year. He added that the administration is seeking a $1 million increase in voluntary contributions to the OAS this year. Nogues responded positively, and commented that the headquarter’s bureaucracy is like a cancer.

10. Ambassador Middendorf praised Paraguay’s emphasis on the private sector which has proved a model for development. Nogues agreed that the GOP’s philosophy favors the free market and private enterprise. Both were of the opinion that good business relations are important in international relations. Middendorf said he was pleased at the prospects for U.S. business in Paraguay, and emphasized that Allis-Chalmers is an important and influential company. Minister Nogues replied that Allis-Chalmers has excellent prospects of winning the turbine contract at the Yacyreta project, and that in Paraguay there is no complex against “Yankee imperialism.” Middendorf gave the Minister copies of his speech on “The Reagan Administration and Economic Development in the Third World” and the USTR statement on U.S. trade policy. The conversation concluded with a discussion of Paraguay’s potential as world breadbasket, its projects to increase production and transport facilities for soybean and other foodstuffs, and complementary OAS projects to benefit small farmers.

11. Meeting with businessmen. On July 23, Ambassador Middendorf met for coffee at the residence with twelve prominent local U.S. and Paraguayan business executives. He described the Reagan administration’s objective of maintaining close and friendly relations with Paraguay and all other nations in the region. He also explained the Caribbean Basin initiative, and emphasized the administration’s belief that the private sector should continue to play a leading role in the economic development of the region. See septel for report of the businessmen’s comments concerning the problems of doing business locally.

12. Visits to OAS/IDB project. In addition to briefings on OAS and IDB projects in Paraguay which he received at their respective local offices, Ambassador Middendorf made a field trip on July 23 to an integrated rural development project in the Department of Paraguari (about one hour’s drive
southeast of Asuncion) which was designed by the OAS and will be financed by a $31 million IDB loan in cooperation with the GOP. The project is aimed at improving agriculture, developing small byproduct industries, and providing service infrastructure (roads, electricity, health, education) for some 60,000 people in the project area. Ambassador Middendorf spoke to both local and OAS/IDB officials to emphasize the importance of timely implementation, cost-control and the multiplier effect of private sector involvement to assure the future success of this and other projects.

13. Other activities. Other activities in Ambassador Middendorf’s crowded schedule included a supper hosted by Ambassador Lane at which presidential confidant and counselor Conrado Pappalardo presented a long and highly partisan account of Paraguay’s troubled political history. Ambassador Middendorf was able deftly to underscore the legitimacy of the non-communist opposition in democratic development and the seriously adverse impact of allegations of widespread corruption—whether well-founded or not—on Paraguay’s image abroad. At a luncheon in his honor hosted by the Foreign Minister and attended also by the Ministers of Interior, Industry and Commerce, and Education as well as prominent Colorado Party legislators, Middendorf heard further discourses on Paraguay’s political situation and economic prospects including its encouragement of foreign—especially U.S.—investment. In this regard the Minister of Industry and Commerce noted that no foreign enterprise has ever been expropriated in Paraguay. In response to reaffirmations of Paraguay’s steadfast anti-communist stance and friendship for the U.S., Middendorf again emphasized U.S. friendship for Paraguay, support for this country’s private sector emphasis in national development, and determination to deal with the threat of communism in Latin America. He again noted the important role that a non-communist opposition can play in a democratic society. In both these affairs, Middendorf reiterated U.S. support for Allis-Chalmers. In his final activity, Ambassador Middendorf attended the formal inauguration of the fourth international cattle show as the special guest of President Stroessner.

14. Press coverage. Ambassador Middendorf’s visit received wide coverage in the press, with front page photos and articles appearing in all major dailies. There was considerable conjecture before and during the visit as to its purpose and its meaning. An editorial in government-line La Tribuna published the day before Middendorf’s arrival stated that the visit showed “the importance that the U.S. gives to relations with our country” and that it was a reward for Paraguay’s constant support of U.S. foreign policy. It was also anticipated
that from this improvement in political relations “mutual economic benefits” could follow. Other papers echoed the thought that the visit signaled an improvement in U.S.-Paraguayan relations. Speculation that the Ambassador was on a secret mission to orchestrate the isolation of Cuba was muted, probably as a result of his strong denial carried in wire service reports from Buenos Aires.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810352–0125. Confidential; Immediate; Eyes only to USOAS.

In telegram 2582 from Asuncion, July 8, the Embassy reported that Paraguayan officials had been informed of the U.S. decision to approve an MDB loan for Paraguay based on “progress noted in our 1980 annual human rights report of Paraguay.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810318–1024)

In telegram 3021 from Asuncion, August 6, the Embassy reported on Middendorf’s July 23 meeting with businessmen in Paraguay. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810367–1183)
